cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Tamil diaspora worldwide
description: Pongal is the most important Tamil harvest festival, celebrated over four days in mid-January (Thai month). It marks the end of the winter solstice and the beginning of Uttarayan (sun's northward journey). Day 1 — Bhogi Pongal: old and unused items are burned in bonfires. Day 2 — Thai Pongal (main day): fresh rice is cooked in a new clay pot with milk, jaggery, and sugarcane until it overflows — the overflow symbolises abundance and prosperity. The phrase 'Pongal-o-Pongal!' is chanted. Day 3 — Mattu Pongal: cattle are decorated with garlands, painted horns, and bells and are worshipped. Day 4 — Kaanum Pongal: family visits and outings. Traditional foods include sakkarai pongal (sweet rice), ven pongal (savoury rice), and sugarcane.
evidence_text: Pongal is a four-day Tamil harvest festival in January. The central ritual on Thai Pongal (Day 2) involves cooking freshly harvested rice with milk in a clay pot until it overflows, symbolising prosperity. Cattle are honoured on Mattu Pongal (Day 3). Foods include sakkarai pongal and ven pongal.
known_limitations: Pongal customs vary slightly between Tamil Nadu districts and Sri Lankan Tamil communities. Modern celebrations in diaspora communities may differ from traditional practices.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Tamil diaspora
description: Kolam (also spelled kolangal) is a traditional Tamil floor art created at the threshold of homes early each morning. It is drawn using white rice flour, chalk powder, or coloured powders in intricate geometric, floral, and figurative patterns. Kolam designs are primarily based on a grid of dots (pulli kolam) around which lines loop and interconnect. The practice is daily — wiped away and redrawn each morning — and is considered to bring prosperity, ward off evil, and welcome guests. Special elaborate kolams are made for festivals like Pongal, Karthigai Deepam, and weddings. Kolam is primarily practised by Tamil women and girls.
evidence_text: Kolam is a traditional Tamil floor art drawn at the entrance of homes using rice flour in intricate geometric patterns based on a grid of dots (pulli kolam). It is redrawn daily as a symbol of prosperity and welcome. Special kolams are made for Pongal, Karthigai Deepam, and weddings.
source_title: UNESCO — Kolam: Living Art of Tamil Nadu
known_limitations: While primarily a Tamil practice, similar traditions exist in other South Indian states under different names (rangoli in North India, muggu in Andhra Pradesh). Kolam designs carry varying regional and community-specific meanings.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), especially Madurai, Pudukkottai, Tiruchirappalli districts
description: Jallikattu (also called Eruthazhuvuthal) is a traditional Tamil bull-taming sport practised during Pongal celebrations, particularly on Mattu Pongal. A bull is released into a crowd and participants attempt to hold on to its hump for a prescribed distance or time. It is considered a symbol of Tamil cultural identity and bravery. Historically it was also used to identify strong bulls for breeding. The sport has been at the centre of legal and political controversy in India. In 2017, the Tamil Nadu government passed the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Tamil Nadu Amendment) Act legalising Jallikattu.
evidence_text: Jallikattu is a traditional Tamil bull-taming sport held during Pongal, especially in Madurai and surrounding districts. Participants grasp a bull's hump as it runs through a crowd. It is a symbol of Tamil cultural identity and has been the subject of legal controversy in India.
source_title: The Hindu — Jallikattu: A Cultural Tradition
known_limitations: Jallikattu is geographically concentrated in specific Tamil Nadu districts; it is not practised across all of Tamil Nadu or by all Tamil communities. Animal welfare concerns remain a topic of ongoing debate.

topic: Kanchipuram Silk Saree — Tamil Textile Heritage
cultural_region: Kanchipuram (Kanchi), Tamil Nadu, India
description: Kanchipuram silk sarees (Kanjivaram sarees) are hand-woven silk sarees produced in the town of Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu. They are distinguished by their heavy silk fabric woven with gold or silver zari (metallic thread), bold contrasting colours for the body and border, and characteristic designs including temples (koil), checks (kattam), and peacocks. The weaving tradition has been practised for over 400 years by the Devanga and Mudaliar weaver communities. Kanchipuram sarees are GI (Geographical Indication) protected. They are considered essential bridal wear in South Indian Hindu weddings.
evidence_text: Kanchipuram silk sarees are hand-woven in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, using heavy silk with gold or silver zari thread. Features include contrasting body and border colours and motifs such as temples, checks, and peacocks. GI-tagged and considered essential bridal wear in South Indian weddings.
source_title: Geographical Indications Registry India — Kanchipuram Silk Saree
known_limitations: Kanchipuram sarees are specific to the Kanchipuram region. Many imitations exist. Not all South Indian women wear Kanjivaram sarees, and wearing a silk saree does not identify a person's caste or religion.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Tamil diaspora
description: Karthigai Deepam is a Tamil festival of lights celebrated in the Tamil month of Karthigai (November–December). It involves lighting rows of clay oil lamps (vilakkus) at the entrance of homes and temples. The most spectacular observance is at Thiruvannamalai, where a massive flame is lit on top of Arunachala hill visible for miles. Karthigai Deepam predates Diwali in the Tamil calendar and is specifically a Tamil and ancient Dravidian tradition. The festival commemorates the legend of the flame of Shiva appearing as an infinite column of light.
evidence_text: Karthigai Deepam is a Tamil festival of lights in November–December, celebrated by lighting clay oil lamps at home entrances and temples. The centrepiece is the giant flame on Arunachala hill at Thiruvannamalai. It is an ancient Dravidian festival predating Diwali in the Tamil calendar.
known_limitations: Karthigai Deepam is specifically Tamil and should not be conflated with Diwali, which is a different festival celebrated by different communities.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Tamil diaspora
description: Carnatic music is the classical music tradition of South India, shared by Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam speaking communities. In Tamil Nadu it is central to cultural life. The tradition is built on ragas (melodic frameworks), talas (rhythmic cycles), and compositions by composers such as Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri (the Trinity of Carnatic music). Instruments include the violin, veena, mridangam (barrel drum), ghatam (clay pot), and kanjira. The music season (Margazhi) in Chennai during December–January features hundreds of concerts at sabhas (music halls) including the famous December Music Season.
evidence_text: Carnatic music is the classical music tradition of South India, central to Tamil cultural life. It is based on ragas and talas, with key composers including Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri. Instruments include veena, mridangam, and violin. The Chennai December Music Season features hundreds of concerts.
known_limitations: Carnatic music is shared across multiple South Indian linguistic communities (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam). The tradition's roots, compositions, and instruments are common to all; regional styles and repertoire differ.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), originating from temple traditions; practised by Tamil communities worldwide
description: Bharatanatyam is one of the oldest Indian classical dance forms, originating from the Devadasi temple dance tradition (Sadir) in Tamil Nadu. It was codified in the Natya Shastra and the Abhinaya Darpana. The dance comprises nritta (pure rhythmic movement), nritya (expressive dance), and natya (dramatic element). Key elements include intricate footwork (adavus), hand gestures (mudras), expressive face and eye movements (abhinaya), and the characteristic bent-knee posture (aramandi). Costumes include a pleated silk dress with a fan-like pleat at the front, jewellery, and make-up. The Arangetram is the formal debut performance of a student.
evidence_text: Bharatanatyam is a Tamil classical dance originating from Devadasi temple traditions in Tamil Nadu. It comprises pure rhythm (nritta), expression (nritya), and drama (natya) with intricate footwork, mudras, and abhinaya. The Arangetram is a student's formal debut. Costumes include pleated silk and traditional jewellery.
known_limitations: Bharatanatyam originated in Tamil Nadu but is now practised across India and the Tamil diaspora. There are multiple schools (bani) with stylistic differences.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Tamil diaspora
description: A Tamil Hindu wedding (Kalyanam) is a multi-day ceremony. Key rituals include: Nichayathartham (engagement ceremony), Kashi Yatra (groom pretends to leave for Kashi/Varanasi as an ascetic, bride's brother persuades him to marry), Oonjal (bride and groom seated on a swing and fed milk rice), Maalai Maatral (exchange of floral garlands), Mangalya Dharanam (groom ties the sacred yellow-turmeric-dyed thread, mangalsutra, around the bride's neck — the defining moment), Saptapadi (seven steps around the sacred fire), and Nalangu (post-wedding teasing games). The bride traditionally wears a Kanchipuram silk saree and mango-leaf designs drawn in turmeric.
evidence_text: A Tamil Hindu wedding includes key rituals: Kashi Yatra (groom's mock renunciation), Oonjal (swing ceremony), Maalai Maatral (garland exchange), Mangalya Dharanam (tying the sacred thread), Saptapadi (seven steps around fire), and Nalangu (post-wedding games). The bride wears a Kanchipuram silk saree.
known_limitations: Tamil wedding customs vary by caste community, family tradition, and whether the community is from Tamil Nadu or Sri Lanka. The description covers broad Hindu Tamil traditions.

topic: Murugan Temple — Arulmigu Dhandayuthapani Swamy, Palani
cultural_region: Palani, Dindigul District, Tamil Nadu, India
description: The Palani Murugan temple (Arulmigu Dhandayuthapani Swamy Thirukovil) is one of the six abodes (Arupadaiveedu) of Lord Murugan in Tamil Nadu. It is located on a hill called Sivagirisam. The presiding deity Dhandayuthapani holds a staff (dandayudham) and wears the thread of renunciation. Devotees traditionally climb 693 steps to reach the temple. The temple is famous for the Kavadi ritual during Thaipusam, in which devotees carry decorated arched structures (kavadi) as an act of devotion, sometimes with physical penances such as vel (spear) piercings. The temple manages the famous prasadam of Panchamirtham (five-nectar divine food).
evidence_text: The Palani Murugan temple is one of the six sacred abodes of Lord Murugan in Tamil Nadu. Devotees climb 693 steps to reach it. During Thaipusam, the Kavadi ritual is performed — devotees carry decorated arched structures as acts of devotion, sometimes with physical penances. Panchamirtham prasadam is a famous offering here.
known_limitations: Each of the six Murugan temples has distinct traditions and significance. Kavadi practices differ between temples and devotee communities.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Malaysia, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Tamil diaspora worldwide
description: Thaipusam is a Tamil Hindu festival celebrated on the full moon of the Tamil month Thai (January–February) to honour Lord Murugan's receiving of the vel (divine spear) from his mother Parvati. The festival is most dramatically observed in Malaysia (Batu Caves) and Singapore and at Palani in Tamil Nadu. Devotees undertake penance including fasting, carrying milk pots (paal kudam), and the Kavadi — a decorated yoke carried on the shoulders, sometimes attached to the body with hooks and skewers. Devotees in a devotional trance are believed to feel no pain during the piercing.
evidence_text: Thaipusam is a Tamil Hindu festival in January–February honouring Lord Murugan's receipt of the vel spear. Devotees carry milk pots and Kavadis — decorated yokes sometimes attached to the body with hooks. Major observances are at Batu Caves (Malaysia), Singapore, and Palani (Tamil Nadu).
known_limitations: Thaipusam is practised differently in Tamil Nadu, Malaysia, Singapore, Sri Lanka, and Mauritius. The physical penance aspects (hooks, skewers) are more prominent in Malaysia and Singapore than in India.

cultural_region: Madurai, Tamil Nadu, India
description: The Arulmigu Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple in Madurai is one of the most iconic temples in India. It is dedicated to Goddess Meenakshi (a form of Parvati) and Lord Sundareswarar (Shiva). The temple complex covers 45 acres and contains 14 gopurams (ornate towers), the tallest being 52 metres high and decorated with thousands of painted stucco figures. The temple is a living example of Dravidian architecture with its characteristic multi-tiered towers, mandapams (pillared halls), and sacred tanks (Porthamarai Kulam — Golden Lotus Tank). It is a major pilgrimage site and one of Tamil Nadu's most-visited monuments.
evidence_text: The Meenakshi Amman Temple in Madurai covers 45 acres with 14 gopurams (the tallest at 52 metres) decorated with thousands of painted stucco figures. It exemplifies Dravidian architecture with towers, mandapams, and a sacred golden lotus tank. It is a major pilgrimage site.
source_title: Archaeological Survey of India — Meenakshi Temple
known_limitations: The temple is of religious significance specifically to Hindu Tamil devotees. The description of the temple should not be extended to make claims about all Tamil or all Hindu culture.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu and broader South India
description: Dravidian architecture is the style of Hindu temple architecture developed in South India, particularly in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala. Its key features include: gopuram (towering ornate gateways over temple entrances, tapering and richly sculptured), vimana (tower above the main shrine), mandapa (pillared hall), garbhagriha (sanctum sanctorum), and sacred tank (pushkarini). The gopurams are covered with colourful plaster sculptures of deities, mythological figures, and decorative motifs. Major examples include the Meenakshi Temple (Madurai), Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur — UNESCO World Heritage Site), and Nataraja Temple (Chidambaram).
evidence_text: Dravidian temple architecture features gopurams (ornate gate towers), vimanas (towers above shrines), mandapas (pillared halls), and sacred tanks. Gopurams are covered with colourful plaster sculptures. Major Tamil Nadu examples include Meenakshi Temple (Madurai) and Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur, UNESCO listed).
source_title: UNESCO World Heritage — Great Living Chola Temples
known_limitations: Dravidian architecture has evolved over 1500+ years with considerable regional variation. Tamil architecture specifically differs from Karnataka Hoysala or Andhra Chalukya styles within the broader Dravidian category.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India) and ancient Tamil kingdoms
description: Sangam literature (Cankam ilakkiyam) refers to the body of classical Tamil poetry composed approximately between 300 BCE and 300 CE, considered among the oldest surviving literary works in any language. The corpus comprises about 2,381 poems collected in eight anthologies (Ettuthokai) and ten idylls (Pattupattu). Sangam poetry is classified by akam (love poetry, interior landscape) and puram (war and public life, exterior landscape). The akam poems use the tinai system — five landscapes (kurinji: hills, mullai: forests, marutham: farmlands, neytal: coastal, palai: desert) each associated with specific love themes, seasons, birds, and flowers.
evidence_text: Sangam literature is classical Tamil poetry from 300 BCE–300 CE, one of the world's oldest literary corpora. Its 2,381 poems cover akam (love, using five landscape-based tinai themes) and puram (war and public life). The five tinais: kurinji (hills), mullai (forests), marutham (farmlands), neytal (coastal), palai (desert).
known_limitations: Sangam literature represents a specific classical period (300 BCE–300 CE). The Tamil literary tradition continued to evolve significantly in subsequent centuries through Bhakti poetry, medieval texts, and modern literature.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India) and Tamil-speaking communities worldwide
description: The Thirukural (Thiruvalluvar's Kural) is a classical Tamil text composed by the poet Thiruvalluvar, estimated to date between 1st century BCE and 5th century CE. It comprises 1,330 couplets (kurals) arranged in 133 chapters of 10 couplets each, grouped in three books: Aram (Virtue/Dharma), Porul (Wealth/Politics), and Inbam (Love). The Thirukural addresses universal ethical principles, statecraft, and love and is revered across religious communities (Hindu, Jain, secular). It has been translated into over 80 languages. Statues of Thiruvalluvar are placed at important locations across Tamil Nadu, and a 133-foot statue stands at Kanyakumari.
evidence_text: The Thirukural by Thiruvalluvar is a classical Tamil text of 1,330 ethical couplets in three books: Aram (Virtue), Porul (Wealth), and Inbam (Love). Dating to around 1st–5th century CE, it is revered across religious communities and translated into 80+ languages. A 133-foot Thiruvalluvar statue stands at Kanyakumari.
known_limitations: The dating of the Thirukural and its author Thiruvalluvar is a matter of scholarly debate. The text is revered across communities and does not belong exclusively to any one religious group.

cultural_region: Chidambaram, Tamil Nadu, India
description: The Natyanjali Dance Festival is an annual classical dance festival held at the Nataraja Temple in Chidambaram during Masi Magam (February–March). Dancers from across India and abroad perform Bharatanatyam and other classical dance forms at the temple complex as an offering to Lord Nataraja (Shiva as the Lord of Dance). The festival draws hundreds of performers and is considered a significant event in the classical dance calendar. The Nataraja Temple is itself a centre of temple dance tradition and the site of the Chidambaram school of Bharatanatyam.
evidence_text: The Natyanjali Dance Festival at the Nataraja Temple in Chidambaram is held during Masi Magam. Dancers perform Bharatanatyam as an offering to Lord Nataraja (Shiva as Lord of Dance). Hundreds of performers from across India and abroad participate.
known_limitations: The Natyanjali Festival is specific to Chidambaram. Temple dance festivals occur at other Tamil Nadu temples with different names, dates, and traditions.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), South India broadly
description: The veena (or vina) is a plucked string instrument central to Carnatic classical music and Tamil culture. The Saraswati veena, most commonly played in Tamil Nadu, has 24 frets set on a large resonating gourd bowl, a long neck, and a resonating chamber at the other end. It produces a distinctly rich, resonant tone. Saraswati, the goddess of knowledge and arts, is iconographically depicted holding a veena. The instrument requires years of dedicated training. Distinguished Tamil veena players include Karaikudi Sambasiva Iyer and the Karaikudi Brothers.
evidence_text: The Saraswati veena is a plucked string instrument with 24 frets, a gourd resonator, and a long neck, central to Carnatic music and Tamil culture. Goddess Saraswati is depicted playing the veena. It is associated with the Karaikudi school of veena playing in Tamil Nadu.
known_limitations: The veena is played across South India, not exclusively in Tamil Nadu. Different veena types exist (Rudra veena, Saraswati veena, etc.) with different associations.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), South India broadly, Tamil diaspora
description: The mridangam is a double-headed barrel drum that is the primary percussion instrument in Carnatic classical music. It is made from jackwood with drumheads of goat or buffalo skin. The left head (thoppi) produces a lower bass sound, while the right head (valanthalai) produces melodic tones through a black paste (soru) applied to the drumhead. The mridangam provides the rhythmic backbone (tala) for Carnatic vocal and instrumental performances. It is also used in temple music and Bharatanatyam accompaniment. The Thanjavur style of mridangam playing is particularly celebrated.
evidence_text: The mridangam is a double-headed barrel drum and the primary percussion instrument in Carnatic music. Made from jackwood with animal skin heads, it provides rhythmic tala. The Thanjavur style of mridangam playing is celebrated. It is also used in temple music and Bharatanatyam.
known_limitations: The mridangam is shared across South Indian music traditions, not exclusively Tamil. Regional playing styles differ.

topic: Nilgiris — Blue Mountains and Toda Tribes
cultural_region: Nilgiri Hills, Tamil Nadu, India (including Toda, Badaga, Kota, Kurumba, and Irula tribal communities)
description: The Nilgiri Hills (Blue Mountains) in Tamil Nadu are home to several indigenous tribal communities, the most documented being the Toda people. The Toda are a pastoralist community traditionally living in barrel-vaulted stone and bamboo huts (munds), raising water buffaloes, and performing elaborate dairy rituals. Toda women are known for their distinctive embroidery (poothkuli) — red and black geometric patterns on white cloth. Toda men traditionally wear a similar patterned cloak (puthukulam). The Toda have an oral poetic tradition and elaborate death and marriage ceremonies. The Nilgiris as a whole was inscribed as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.
evidence_text: The Nilgiri Hills in Tamil Nadu are home to the Toda, a pastoralist tribal community raising water buffaloes. Toda women create distinctive poothkuli embroidery (red-black geometric patterns on white cloth). The Nilgiris is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.
known_limitations: The Nilgiris has multiple tribal communities (Toda, Badaga, Kota, Kurumba, Irula) with distinct cultures. The Toda are the most internationally documented but should not be treated as representative of all Nilgiri hill communities.

cultural_region: Chettinad region, Sivaganga District, Tamil Nadu, India
description: Chettinad cuisine is the cooking tradition of the Nattukotai Chettiars (Nagarathar), a merchant community from the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu. It is known for its bold flavours, use of freshly ground spice blends, and availability of ingredients from across the trading routes the Chettiars maintained in Southeast Asia. Key spices include kalpasi (stone flower), marathi mokku, and star anise. Signature dishes include Chettinad chicken curry, Kavuni arisi (black rice pudding), Paniyaram, and Kavuni maavu. The cuisine is predominantly non-vegetarian but has a rich vegetarian tradition.
evidence_text: Chettinad cuisine from the Nattukotai Chettiar community of Tamil Nadu is known for bold flavours, freshly ground spices (including kalpasi stone flower), and influences from Southeast Asian trade routes. Signature dishes include Chettinad chicken curry, Kavuni arisi (black rice pudding), and Paniyaram.
known_limitations: Chettinad cuisine is specific to the Nattukotai Chettiar community; it is not representative of all Tamil cuisine. Tamil cuisine varies by district, community, and occasion.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Tamil diaspora worldwide
description: Tamil New Year (Puthandu or Tamil Puthuvarudam) is celebrated on the first day of the Tamil month Chittirai, which falls on April 14 each year (Vaisakhi in other traditions). On the morning of Puthandu, families arrange a special tray (kani) with auspicious items — fruits, flowers, betel leaves, gold, silver, and the faces of deities — which is the first thing one looks upon on waking (Kani Darshan). Special foods include mango pachadi (a mixture of sweet, sour, and bitter tastes symbolising the different flavours of life) and Puthandu Pachadi. Traditional new-year wishes are 'Puthandu Vazthukal!'
evidence_text: Tamil New Year (Puthandu) is on April 14 each year. Families view an auspicious tray (kani) of fruits, flowers, gold, and deity images as the first sight on waking (Kani Darshan). Special foods include mango pachadi (representing life's varied flavours). Greetings: 'Puthandu Vazthukal!'
known_limitations: The Tamil New Year is on April 14; this differs from Hindu lunar new years celebrated in other parts of India. Tamil diaspora communities in different countries celebrate Puthandu on the same date.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Tamil diaspora; historically across Tamil kingdoms
description: Silambam is a Tamil weapon-based martial art using a long bamboo staff (silambam kol). It is one of the oldest martial arts in India, referenced in Sangam literature and ancient Tamil texts. The practice involves rhythmic striking patterns, footwork, and multiple staff techniques. Traditionally practised in Tamil Nadu's villages and used in historical warfare, Silambam also has forms using other weapons (knife, shield, etc.). Modern Silambam has been proposed for Olympic inclusion.
evidence_text: Silambam is an ancient Tamil martial art using a bamboo staff (silambam kol), referenced in Sangam literature. It involves rhythmic striking patterns and footwork. Practised in Tamil Nadu villages and used historically in Tamil warfare. Modern forms include knife and shield variants.
source_title: Sangam Period References and Tamil Nadu Sports Authority
known_limitations: Historical details about Silambam's origins come from Sangam literature references that require scholarly interpretation. Current institutional sources are limited. The art is not uniformly practised across all Tamil Nadu districts.

cultural_region: Southern Tamil Nadu (Tirunelveli, Kanyakumari, Tuticorin districts), Sri Lanka
description: The Nadar community (historically Shanar) is a Tamil community traditionally associated with the palmyra palm (panai) cultivation and toddy-tapping in southern Tamil Nadu. The palmyra palm is the state tree of Tamil Nadu and plays a central role in the culture of southern Tamil districts — its products include neera (sweet palm sap), karupatti (palm jaggery), panangkizhangu (palmyra tuber), and various handicrafts from its leaves and trunk. The Nadar community has a rich tradition of palm-leaf manuscript writing. They rose to prominence in the 19th–20th centuries through education and commerce.
evidence_text: The palmyra palm is the state tree of Tamil Nadu and central to the culture of southern Tamil districts. Its products include neera (palm sap), karupatti (palm jaggery), and palmyra tuber. Palm-leaf manuscript writing (palm-leaf books) is an associated tradition.
source_title: Tamil Nadu State Government — State Symbols
known_limitations: Palm-leaf culture is specific to southern Tamil Nadu and is not representative of all Tamil communities. The Nadar community's specific history involves complex social and caste dynamics that should not be oversimplified.

cultural_region: Thiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu, India
description: Arunachala is a sacred hill in Thiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu, believed to be a manifestation of Lord Shiva as a column of fire. The Annamalai Temple at its base is one of the largest temple complexes in the world (covering 25 acres). Devotees circumambulate the hill (Girivalam) on foot (approximately 14 km), especially on full moon nights when thousands gather. The hill was the home of the 20th-century Tamil saint and philosopher Ramana Maharshi, whose ashram (Ramanasramam) is here. Karthigai Deepam's giant beacon flame is lit on top of Arunachala.
evidence_text: Arunachala sacred hill in Thiruvannamalai is believed to be Shiva manifested as a column of fire. Devotees circumambulate it (Girivalam, 14 km) especially on full moon nights. The Annamalai Temple covers 25 acres. Ramana Maharshi's ashram is here. Karthigai Deepam's beacon flame is lit on the hill.
known_limitations: Arunachala's religious significance is specific to the Shaiva tradition. The hill is sacred primarily to Shaivite Hindus; it may not hold the same significance for Tamil communities of different religious backgrounds.

cultural_region: Tamil Nadu (India), Tamil communities in Sri Lanka
description: Tamil women traditionally wear elaborate gold jewellery, a significant part of their cultural and bridal identity. The Muthu Kuzhal (pearl ear ornament) is one among a rich tradition of Tamil gold jewellery forms including: Jhumka (dangling bell-shaped earrings), Kammal (ear stud), Maatal (a piece linking ear to hair), Thali (mangalsutra — sacred marriage thread in gold), Vanki (upper-arm bracelet), Bajuband, Padakam (pendant necklace), and Oddiyanam (waist belt). Temple jewellery, originally created for temple deities, is worn during classical dance performances. Antique Tamil gold jewellery forms are documented by the Tanjavur district.
evidence_text: Tamil women wear rich gold jewellery traditions including Jhumka earrings, Maatal (ear-to-hair ornament), Thali (sacred marriage thread), Vanki (upper-arm bracelet), and Oddiyanam (waist belt). Temple jewellery, made for deities, is also worn in Bharatanatyam. Tanjavur district documents antique Tamil gold jewellery forms.
source_title: Tanjavur District Cultural Heritage — Tamil Jewellery
known_limitations: Tamil gold jewellery traditions vary by region, community, and economic context. Jewellery alone does not identify a person's cultural background conclusively.

topic: Eelam Tamil Culture — Sri Lankan Tamil Heritage
cultural_region: Northern and Eastern Sri Lanka (Jaffna, Batticaloa, Trincomalee); Sri Lankan Tamil diaspora worldwide
description: Sri Lankan Tamil communities (Eelam Tamils) have a distinct cultural identity with shared roots in Tamil Nadu but with unique features developed over centuries of settlement in Sri Lanka. Key cultural elements: the Jaffna Tamil dialect differs from standard Tamil; Nallur Kandaswamy Temple in Jaffna is a major religious centre; the Chariot Festival (Ther Festival) at Nallur draws hundreds of thousands of devotees; the Karadayan Nombu is an observance unique to Tamil women in the Jaffna tradition; traditional architecture in Jaffna uses a distinctive courtyard-house (tharavadu) style; Jaffna cuisine includes unique dishes like crab curry with coconut milk and Jaffna mutton curry.
evidence_text: Sri Lankan Tamils (Eelam Tamils) have a distinct cultural identity with the Jaffna dialect, the Nallur Kandaswamy Temple (major pilgrimage centre), annual Chariot Festival, Karadayan Nombu observance, courtyard-house (tharavadu) architecture, and unique Jaffna cuisine including crab curry.
known_limitations: Sri Lankan Tamil culture was deeply affected by decades of civil conflict (1983–2009). Cultural practices and community demographics have been significantly disrupted. This record provides pre-conflict and contemporary cultural context; it is not comprehensive.
